paragraphs: When different classification mistakes carry different costs, choosing the most likely label is not the whole problem. The learner needs to choose a label with low expected cost while limiting how much labeling information it requests. This paper introduces COAL, an active learning algorithm designed for this cost-sensitive, multiclass setting.

COAL learns regression models for the costs associated with individual labels and predicts the label with the smallest estimated cost. To decide what to query, it considers a collection of regressors that fit previous observations well. Their predictions indicate which labels could still be the cheapest. Labels that are already ruled out as winners do not receive queries.

The authors prove efficient implementation is possible for regression families that support squared-loss optimization, alongside guarantees for prediction quality and labeling effort. Their experiment reports significant improvements in labeling effort and test cost over passive and active alternatives. The contribution connects selective information gathering directly to the decision that matters: finding the least costly label.
icml-2017-active-learning-for-cost-sensi.tldr: COAL reduces labeling effort by querying only labels that could have the lowest prediction cost.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction when examples arrive sequentially and the learner observes only selected features of each example. On every round, it chooses coordinates, predicts a numerical outcome, and then receives the true label and a squared-error loss. The feature vectors may be chosen adversarially, making feature selection part of the learning challenge.

The target is sublinear regret against the best sparse linear predictor chosen after seeing all the data. This means the accumulated disadvantage relative to that predictor grows more slowly than the number of rounds. Without assumptions, obtaining an efficient solution is computationally intractable. The authors instead assume the data matrix satisfies the restricted isometry property, a structural condition concerning sparse directions.

Under that assumption, they obtain computationally efficient algorithms with sublinear regret for two versions of the problem. One generates labels from a sparse linear model with additive Gaussian noise; the other allows adversarial labels. The result shows how the stated structural assumption enables efficient learning even with selective feature observation and, in the second variant, adversarial outcomes.
icml-2017-adaptive-feature-selection-com.tldr: A restricted isometry assumption enables efficient online sparse regression with sublinear regret despite selective feature observation.

paragraphs: Co-clustering groups data instances and their features at the same time. The aim is to find groups that make sense together: a useful partition of examples can depend on which features are grouped, and vice versa. This paper develops an unsupervised method that connects these two partitions through optimal transport.

The method constructs empirical measures over instances and features, then computes an entropy-regularized transport coupling between them. The resulting matrix represents an estimated joint probability distribution connecting the two sides. A further factorization, using representations at multiple scales, turns that matrix into row and column partitions. The coupling therefore supplies a shared intermediate description from which both clusterings are derived.

The authors justify this construction through a variational inference interpretation of regularized optimal transport. They also introduce a kernelized version based on Gromov-Wasserstein distance. Both algorithms can automatically determine the numbers of row and column clusters. Extensive experiments demonstrate the reported speed and accuracy, supporting transport-based joint modeling as a practical approach to co-clustering.
icml-2017-co-clustering-through-optimal-.tldr: An optimal transport coupling links instances and features so their clusters and cluster counts can be learned together.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a conditional accelerated lazy stochastic gradient descent algorithm. Its stated contribution concerns the amount of optimization work needed to reach a target accuracy. The analysis focuses on calls to a stochastic first-order oracle: a source of gradient information used by the optimization procedure to choose how to update its current solution.

The authors report an optimal number of calls to that oracle and a convergence rate expressed as O(1/epsilon²), where epsilon represents the desired accuracy. They compare this with an earlier projection-free stochastic gradient method based on Online Frank-Wolfe, whose stated rate is O(1/epsilon⁴). The difference is in the exponent governing dependence on accuracy, rather than merely a constant multiplier.

That distinction matters when increasingly precise solutions are required: the reported bound grows less sharply as epsilon becomes smaller. The abstract presents this as a theoretical improvement over the specified earlier method. Its concrete finding is the improved accuracy dependence together with oracle-call optimality; the reported result concerns these optimization guarantees rather than a measured application-specific speedup.
icml-2017-conditional-accelerated-lazy-s.tldr: The proposed stochastic optimization algorithm achieves optimal oracle-call complexity and improves the stated accuracy dependence from O(1/epsilon⁴) to O(1/epsilon²).

paragraphs: Online clustering must accommodate new points as they arrive. Existing decisions may be revisable, but changing them can be expensive. This paper formalizes that tension as consistent k-clustering: maintain a clustering whose objective stays within a constant factor of the optimum while making as few clustering changes as possible.

The authors establish a worst-case lower bound of Omega(k log n) changes for a broad range of objectives, where n is the number of arriving points. Thus, some amount of revision is unavoidable. They also give an algorithm requiring only O(k² log⁴ n) changes while retaining a constant competitive guarantee. This sharply reduces the dependence on stream length compared with reclustering after every arrival.

Experiments show substantially fewer changes than the theoretical upper bound suggests, with growth approximately logarithmic in n. That observed behavior is distinct from the worst-case guarantee. Together, the results make stability an explicit algorithmic objective and show that maintaining good clusters need not require continuously revising the clustering whenever another point appears.
icml-2017-consistent-k-clustering-6e361f.tldr: Consistent k-clustering maintains a constant-factor clustering approximation while provably limiting how often the clustering changes.

paragraphs: Learning causal relationships through interventions raises a design question: which interventions should be performed when their costs matter? This paper assumes the graph's skeleton is given. The skeleton specifies which variables are connected but leaves the directions of causal relationships unresolved. The task is to choose interventions that determine those directions.

The authors seek a minimum-total-cost intervention set that can uniquely identify any causal graph consistent with the supplied skeleton. They show that this cost-optimal design problem can be solved in polynomial time. The identification requirement is significant because the intervention set must work across the possible directed graphs sharing that skeleton.

They then study the additional restriction of a limited number of interventions. For this setting, they provide polynomial-time algorithms when the skeleton is a tree or a clique tree. For general chordal skeletons, they develop an efficient greedy algorithm, with improvements available for interval graphs. The results distinguish minimizing total intervention cost from handling an intervention-count constraint, where the skeleton's structure shapes the available algorithms.
icml-2017-cost-optimal-learning-of-causa.tldr: Given a causal graph's undirected skeleton, the paper designs cost-optimal identifying interventions and studies algorithms for limited intervention budgets.

paragraphs: Clustering quality depends on both how examples are represented and how similarity is measured. This paper studies supervised clustering learning, where labeled partitions provide information about which examples belong together. Its goal is to learn a deep similarity representation that supports good grouping, rather than treating the original representation as fixed.

The authors introduce a new loss function for deep supervised clustering metric learning. A central contribution is a closed-form expression for its gradient, avoiding the iterative gradient computations used by some earlier deep approaches. Computing this gradient scales linearly with training mini-batch size and quadratically with representation dimensionality. These dependencies explain where the method's computational savings arise and which dimensions still affect its cost.

The paper also establishes an interpretation of the method as learning spectral clustering, linking its training objective to that clustering framework. Experiments on standard real-world datasets report state-of-the-art Recall@K performance. The stated contribution combines a learned representation and similarity measure with an efficiently computable training gradient, supported by the reported evaluation results.
icml-2017-deep-spectral-clustering-learn.tldr: A new deep clustering loss enables closed-form gradient computation and achieves reported state-of-the-art Recall@K performance.

paragraphs: A chi-squared independence test asks whether two variables show evidence of a relationship. Making that test differentially private introduces an additional statistical challenge: privacy protection should preserve useful decisions. This paper examines both type-I errors, which falsely indicate dependence, and type-II errors, which miss dependence that is present.

The proposed unit circle mechanism uses geometric properties of the test statistics. Compared with existing output-perturbation mechanisms, the authors report improving the specified term in the type-II error from O(1) to O(exp(-sqrt(N))), where N is sample size. That term therefore decreases with more data instead of remaining constant in order. This is a claim about a component of the error analysis, not a statement that every source of testing error disappears.

The paper also develops procedures for multiple chi-squared tests by combining the mechanism with the sparse vector technique and the exponential mechanism. These procedures control the family-wise error rate, addressing false positives across a collection of tests. The contribution connects privacy-preserving testing with both sensitivity to real relationships and error control across multiple decisions.
icml-2017-differentially-private-chi-squ.tldr: A geometry-based private chi-squared mechanism improves a type-II error term and supports family-wise error control for multiple tests.

paragraphs: Evaluating a probabilistic model helps determine how it should be revised. Predictive accuracy is one useful signal, but it does not fully describe how a model explains its observations. This paper proposes examining posterior dispersion to reveal difficulties that a prediction-focused evaluation may not make apparent.

The idea is to assess each data point in relation to posterior uncertainty about the model's hidden structure. Rather than producing only another overall accuracy score, this perspective asks how individual observations fare against uncertainty in the inferred explanation of the data. The authors formalize the approach through a family of posterior dispersion indices, or PDI. These indices are intended to complement the information supplied by poorly predicted observations.

The paper demonstrates how a PDI reveals patterns of model mismatch in voting preferences, supermarket shopping, and population genetics. Such patterns can guide the next round of model development by indicating where the current explanation struggles. The contribution is an additional diagnostic perspective within the modeling cycle, connecting evaluation directly to posterior uncertainty.
icml-2017-evaluating-bayesian-models-wit.tldr: Posterior dispersion indices diagnose model mismatch by examining individual observations in relation to uncertainty about hidden structure.

paragraphs: Generating discrete structures creates a problem that visual plausibility alone cannot solve: an output may violate the rules of its representation. Arithmetic expressions and molecular structures are examples where validity matters. This paper uses the observation that such data can often be expressed as parse trees governed by a context-free grammar.

The proposed variational autoencoder encodes these trees into a latent representation and decodes directly back into parse trees. Building the grammar into this process ensures syntactic validity of generated outputs. That guarantee concerns conformity to the grammar. The authors also report a more coherent latent space, meaning nearby latent points decode into similar discrete outputs.

This organization matters when the latent space is used to search for useful structures. If nearby locations correspond to related outputs, optimization can operate over a representation with meaningful local relationships. The paper demonstrates improved Bayesian optimization performance for symbolic regression and molecule generation. Its findings connect grammatical constraints with both valid generation and a latent representation that better supports the reported search tasks.
icml-2017-grammar-variational-autoencode.tldr: A variational autoencoder operating on grammar parse trees ensures syntactic validity and learns a latent space useful for optimizing discrete structures.

paragraphs: An image's content can stay recognizable even when the image is rotated or translated, yet those changes can disrupt a classifier. This paper introduces TIGraNet, a network designed to learn features that are inherently invariant to isometric transformations. The targeted transformations preserve geometry, with rotation and translation serving as the stated examples.

TIGraNet represents images as signals on graphs. It replaces conventional convolution and pooling operations with graph spectral convolution and dynamic graph pooling. These components jointly contribute to the representation's invariance. The approach places the handling of these geometric changes within the network's representation and operations, making transformation behavior part of the architecture itself.

Experiments report high performance on rotated and translated test images compared with classical architectures that are sensitive to those changes. The authors also report resilience to data variability and sustained performance when training sets are limited. The findings support graph-based invariant features for the studied transformations, connecting architectural structure with classification that remains reliable as image position or orientation changes.
icml-2017-graph-based-isometry-invariant.tldr: TIGraNet uses graph-based image operations to learn features invariant to rotations and translations.

paragraphs: A partially observable Markov decision process describes decisions made with uncertain outcomes and incomplete information. Its usefulness depends on having a suitable model of the environment, which can be difficult to construct. Bayes-adaptive POMDPs incorporate model learning during execution, allowing the agent to account for uncertainty about the model itself.

In principle, this Bayesian formulation supports an optimal balance between exploiting current knowledge and exploring to improve it. Solving the resulting decision problem is computationally difficult, however. The paper adapts POMCP, a Monte Carlo tree search method, to the Bayes-adaptive setting. The resulting algorithm, BA-POMCP, brings that search approach to planning while the environment model is being learned.

The authors show that BA-POMCP handles problems beyond the reach of previous solution methods. They also develop techniques that exploit the structure of Bayes-adaptive POMDPs to make the algorithm more efficient and provide convergence proofs for those techniques. The contribution makes progress toward usable planning under both incomplete observations and model uncertainty, without turning the framework's in-principle optimality into a blanket finite-computation guarantee.
icml-2017-learning-in-pomdps-with-monte-.tldr: BA-POMCP extends Monte Carlo tree search to planning with partial observations and an environment model learned during execution.

paragraphs: Learning a relationship between two data domains often relies on matched examples showing how one corresponds to the other. Collecting those pairs can be costly. This paper instead studies whether useful cross-domain relationships can be discovered from unpaired data, where examples from the two domains are available without explicit example-by-example correspondences.

The authors introduce DiscoGAN, a method based on a generative adversarial network. It learns relations between domains and uses them to transfer style. The important goal is more specific than producing an output that resembles the destination domain: the transformation should also preserve key attributes of the original example. The abstract identifies orientation and face identity as attributes preserved in the reported results.

These findings show that the proposed method can discover useful relationships without the paired supervision usually used to illustrate them. Preserving identity or orientation makes the transferred output meaningfully related to its input. The contribution therefore addresses both the cost of obtaining matched training examples and the need for cross-domain transformations that retain important content.
icml-2017-learning-to-discover-cross-dom.tldr: DiscoGAN learns cross-domain style transfers from unpaired data while preserving key attributes such as orientation and face identity.

paragraphs: Selecting people across populations is difficult when their skills are not directly comparable. This paper defines individual quality through relative standing within a person's own population, using the cumulative distribution value of their skill. That definition creates a common scale for comparing candidates whose underlying abilities are measured differently.

The learner does not know these true relative ranks and must estimate them from a finite candidate pool. The paper studies meritocratic fairness requirements under which selection probability increases monotonically with true quality. It quantifies the loss in selection quality, or regret, associated with satisfying these requirements despite uncertainty about candidates' ranks.

The authors provide algorithms with provable fairness and regret guarantees, together with lower bounds that characterize unavoidable difficulty. Empirical results suggest better performance than the theoretical bounds indicate. They also extend the analysis to repeated batches of new applicants, where previous rounds supply additional comparison data. The result is a formal treatment of fair cross-population selection under a specific definition of merit and uncertainty about that merit.
icml-2017-meritocratic-fairness-for-cros.tldr: The paper quantifies selection-quality tradeoffs when fairness requires higher within-population rank to imply at least as much selection probability.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization becomes expensive when every evaluation requires substantial computation or experimentation. Multi-fidelity methods reduce this burden by using cheaper approximations of the desired function. This paper addresses a setting where approximation quality is adjustable across a continuous space, rather than restricted to a finite menu of choices.

For neural-network tuning, the abstract illustrates this space with the amount of training data and the number of training iterations. Changing either quantity changes the approximation used to assess a candidate configuration. BOCA, the proposed Bayesian optimization method, is designed for this richer setting, where approximation choices have multiple adjustable dimensions.

The authors characterize BOCA theoretically and establish better regret than strategies that ignore the available approximations. They also report that BOCA outperforms several baselines in synthetic and real experiments. These findings support treating the approximation space as part of the optimization problem itself. The central contribution is a method that can use a spectrum of cheaper evaluations to improve the search for a good solution to the expensive target problem.
icml-2017-multi-fidelity-bayesian-optimi.tldr: BOCA uses continuously adjustable approximations to improve Bayesian optimization of expensive black-box functions.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix estimation seeks a matrix with a compact underlying structure. This paper studies greedy methods for that task and supplies new guarantees about how well their solutions approximate the optimization target. The guarantees rely on restricted strong convexity and smoothness, so they apply under stated conditions on the estimation objective.

The analysis also reveals connections between low-rank estimation and combinatorial optimization. In particular, the resulting bounds resemble approximation guarantees from submodular maximization. This is useful conceptually because it connects a matrix estimation problem to a separate body of reasoning about greedy selection. The abstract identifies a resemblance and a theoretical connection, without claiming that all low-rank estimation problems are themselves submodular maximization problems.

Beyond objective approximation, the authors provide statistical recovery guarantees, addressing recovery of the underlying matrix rather than only optimization quality. They also compare greedy estimation with established baselines on two real-world problems. The contribution thus combines an analysis of greedy optimization, a link to combinatorial methods, and statistical guarantees under the stated structural assumptions.
icml-2017-on-approximation-guarantees-fo.tldr: New conditional guarantees connect greedy low-rank matrix estimation with approximation bounds from combinatorial optimization.

paragraphs: PixelCNN models describe natural images probabilistically, but existing versions can devote too much attention to fine image details while overlooking larger structures such as object shapes. Generating images with them can also be computationally expensive. This paper extends the PixelCNN family by introducing auxiliary variables intended to address these two shortcomings.

The authors develop two models using different transformed views of an image. One uses a quantized grayscale representation, while the other uses an image pyramid containing multiple resolutions. These auxiliary representations give the model additional ways to organize image information beyond the original pixel-level description. The distinction between the two models is the image transformation supplying that extra structure.

Experiments demonstrate benefits from the proposed models, especially substantially more realistic-looking samples than previous state-of-the-art probabilistic image models. The reported visual improvement supports the usefulness of incorporating transformed image views into generation. The paper's approach connects probabilistic pixel modeling with representations that expose broader image structure while also tackling the computational burden of the sampling procedure.
icml-2017-pixelcnn-models-with-auxiliary.tldr: Adding grayscale or multiresolution auxiliary representations to PixelCNN produces more realistic image samples in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Personalization asks which treatment option would have the best causal effect for a particular individual. This paper studies that task using passive observations of individual characteristics, assigned treatments, and resulting outcomes. The possible choices are discrete, such as different news items or medical drugs, and the objective is an individualized treatment decision.

A standard approach fits a separate outcome regression for each treatment and compares their predictions. The authors instead formulate personalization as one learning task. Their method recursively partitions the data into regions where different treatments are optimal. They also develop an optimal partitioning extension that finds a globally optimal partition, producing a compact and interpretable personalization model.

The paper additionally introduces tools for validating and evaluating personalization models with observational data. It uses those tools in personalized medicine and job training applications to demonstrate the proposed approaches. The contribution aligns the learned partition with treatment choice, so the model describes which option to select in each region rather than relying solely on separately fitted outcome predictions.
icml-2017-recursive-partitioning-for-per.tldr: The paper learns interpretable treatment-selection partitions directly from observational data and develops tools for evaluating them.

paragraphs: Running machine learning on tiny devices requires controlling memory use, computation, and battery consumption together. This paper introduces Bonsai, a tree-based prediction algorithm designed for hardware as constrained as an Arduino Uno with 2 KB of RAM. The goal is to preserve predictive accuracy while making the model small and inexpensive to evaluate.

Bonsai learns one shallow, sparse tree with expressive nodes. Before the tree operates, a sparse projection maps the input into a low-dimensional space. The projection and all tree parameters are learned jointly. This design makes both the input representation and the predictor part of the same effort to fit a strict resource budget.

Across multiple benchmark datasets, Bonsai predicts in milliseconds on slow microcontrollers and fits in kilobytes of memory. The reported comparisons show lower battery consumption than the other evaluated algorithms and accuracy improvements that can reach 30% over resource-efficient alternatives. In a separate constrained setting, it also improves search results over Bing's L3 ranker with a 300-byte model budget, demonstrating usefulness beyond IoT prediction.
icml-2017-resource-efficient-machine-lea.tldr: Bonsai jointly learns a compact projection and sparse tree to deliver accurate, low-cost predictions on severely memory-constrained devices.

paragraphs: Success on one reinforcement learning task does not automatically produce success on a related task. This paper addresses that transfer problem with Schema Networks, an object-oriented generative simulator of physical dynamics. The proposed architecture aims to learn an environment's dynamics from data while representing causal relationships among events.

Schema Networks can separate multiple causes contributing to an event and reason backward through causes to pursue goals. These capabilities connect prediction of how the environment behaves with planning toward a desired outcome. The structured representation is central to the approach: objects and causal dynamics provide the basis for reasoning across related situations.

The authors compare Schema Networks with Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic and Progressive Networks on a collection of Breakout variations. They report consistently faster, more robust learning and better transfer, including zero-shot generalization in that evaluation. These results support the approach within the tested task family. The broader proposal is that learning causal relationships and generalizing from limited data are important ingredients for more general intelligence.
icml-2017-schema-networks-zero-shot-tran.tldr: Schema Networks learn object-based causal dynamics and show faster learning and better zero-shot transfer across tested Breakout variations.

paragraphs: SplitNet addresses two connected costs of deep networks: storing many parameters and coordinating computation across processors. It learns to organize a network into groups, or a hierarchy of groups, that use disjoint feature sets. The grouping is learned alongside the network weights through assignments linking classes and features to groups.

The resulting network has a tree structure with no connections between branched subtrees serving semantically different class groups. Removing those connections reduces parameters and computation. At prediction time, the subnetworks can be evaluated independently, apart from shared lower-layer weights that can be copied across processors. This structure makes model parallelization straightforward.

The authors evaluate the approach with ResNet and AlexNet on CIFAR-100 and ILSVRC 2012. They report substantially fewer parameters while maintaining comparable or better classification accuracy than the original full networks, along with faster testing using multiple GPUs. The findings show that learned class-and-feature organization can serve both model compression and parallel execution, rather than treating those goals as separate modifications.
icml-2017-splitnet-learning-to-semantica.tldr: SplitNet learns independent semantic branches that reduce network size and enable parallel prediction while retaining strong classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent is attractive because it solves optimization problems through simple coordinate updates. In sparse regression, however, many of those updates may accomplish nothing. This paper focuses on that wasted computation: an algorithm can spend substantial time revisiting coordinates without moving its objective closer to the desired solution.

The proposed StingyCD algorithm skips updates when they are guaranteed not to decrease the objective value. This lets it avoid certified unproductive work while retaining the basic coordinate descent structure. The guarantee also limits how aggressively it can exploit sparsity. The authors therefore introduce StingyCD+, which skips updates more aggressively and achieves additional speedups.

Because both methods make relatively simple changes to coordinate descent, the authors describe them as straightforward to combine with other approaches for scaling optimization. Empirical comparisons on several L1-regularized problems show considerable reductions in convergence time. The main lesson is that identifying work that will not improve the objective can accelerate an otherwise simple optimizer; the more aggressive variant extends that strategy beyond StingyCD's guaranteed-skipping rule.
icml-2017-stingycd-safely-avoiding-waste.tldr: StingyCD speeds coordinate descent by skipping provably unproductive updates, while StingyCD+ skips more aggressively for further gains.

paragraphs: Cubic regularization is an approach to non-convex optimization with attractive convergence properties, including the ability to escape strict saddle points. Its computational cost can nevertheless make it impractical for large learning problems. This paper develops a subsampled version intended to retain those theoretical advantages while reducing the work needed for each optimization step.

The method approximates gradients and Hessians using samples. The key question is how accurate these approximations must be to preserve the behavior of cubic regularization. The authors use concentration inequalities to design a sampling scheme that provides sufficient accuracy, connecting reduced computation to the requirements of the convergence analysis.

They establish that the scheme retains strong global and local convergence guarantees of cubically regularized methods. Here, global convergence describes the optimization guarantee; it is not a claim of finding a global minimum of every non-convex function. Experiments support the theory. The contribution shows how carefully controlled subsampling can reduce the cost of curvature-based optimization without giving up the stated convergence properties.
icml-2017-sub-sampled-cubic-regularizati.tldr: A controlled subsampling scheme reduces cubic regularization's computational cost while preserving its stated global and local convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: A prediction can be explained partly by examining which training examples most influenced it. This paper brings influence functions from robust statistics into that role, tracing a prediction backward through the learning procedure to the training data. The aim is to identify examples that bear the most responsibility for a particular model output.

To make the method practical for modern models, the authors develop an efficient implementation requiring access to gradients and Hessian-vector products. This connects the explanation to the model's training computations. They also investigate approximations on non-convex and non-differentiable models, where the supporting theory no longer applies, and find that these approximations can still provide useful information.

Experiments with linear models and convolutional neural networks demonstrate several uses: interpreting behavior, debugging models, finding dataset errors, and constructing visually indistinguishable training-set attacks. These applications show that influential examples can reveal both useful training signals and vulnerabilities. The empirical usefulness outside the theory's scope is an explicitly qualified result, rather than a general guarantee that every influence estimate is accurate.
icml-2017-understanding-black-box-predic.tldr: Influence functions trace predictions to influential training examples, supporting interpretation, debugging, dataset checks, and analysis of training-set attacks.

paragraphs: Modeling video requires accounting for how visual information is related across both space and time. This paper introduces the Video Pixel Network, or VPN, a probabilistic model of the discrete raw pixel values in a video. Its target is their joint distribution, allowing the model to represent dependencies across the video rather than treating its pixel values independently.

The neural architecture reflects the structure of a video tensor: time, two spatial dimensions, and color. It encodes these relationships as a four-dimensional dependency chain. This design connects the probability model to the organization of the data, so temporal development and within-frame visual structure are represented within the same modeling framework.

On Moving MNIST, the authors report performance approaching the best possible level, a large improvement over prior results, with generated videos differing only slightly from ground truth. On action-conditional Robotic Pushing, VPN produces detailed samples and generalizes to motion involving novel objects. These findings support its ability to capture both image detail and motion in the evaluated settings.
icml-2017-video-pixel-networks-9f09cf3f5.tldr: Video Pixel Networks model joint pixel probabilities across time, space, and color, producing strong results on two video benchmarks.
